question: What is an affidavit?

options.text: A signed written statement, sworn to or affirmed before an authorized officer
options.why: Correct. That's the Department of State's definition.

options.text: An agreement between two parties
options.why: Wrong. That's a contract.

options.text: A notary's record book
options.why: Wrong. A record book isn't a sworn statement.

options.text: A court's final decision
options.why: Wrong. That's a judgment.

explanation: An affidavit is a signed statement, duly sworn to, before an officer authorized to administer oaths.

refs.title: Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: What is the person who makes an affidavit called?

options.text: The affiant (also called the deponent)
options.why: Correct. The maker of an affidavit is the affiant or deponent.

options.text: The grantor
options.why: Wrong. A grantor conveys property in a deed.

options.text: The testator
options.why: Wrong. A testator makes a will.

options.text: The vendee
options.why: Wrong. A vendee is a buyer.

explanation: The person who swears to an affidavit is the affiant or deponent.

refs.title: Definitions: Affiant (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Definitions: Deponent (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: What is a jurat?

options.text: The clause at the end of an affidavit stating when, where and before whom it was sworn
options.why: Correct. The jurat is the officer's certificate of the oath.

options.text: A juror's oath
options.why: Wrong. Jurors take an oath, but that isn't a notarial jurat.

options.text: An acknowledgment certificate
options.why: Wrong. That certifies a different act.

options.text: A statement of the notary's fees
options.why: Wrong. Fees aren't the jurat.

explanation: A jurat is the certificate at the end of an affidavit showing when, where and before whom it was sworn.

refs.title: Definitions: Jurat (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: Which is the form of oath the Department of State booklet gives for an affidavit?

options.text: "Do you solemnly swear that the contents of this affidavit subscribed by you are correct and true?"
options.why: Correct. That's the suggested oath wording.

options.text: "Do you acknowledge that you signed this?"
options.why: Wrong. That's acknowledgment language, not an oath.

options.text: "Is this your handwriting?"
options.why: Wrong. That says nothing about the truth of the contents.

options.text: "Do you agree to these terms?"
options.why: Wrong. That's contract assent, not an oath.

explanation: The booklet suggests: "Do you solemnly swear that the contents of this affidavit subscribed by you are correct and true?"
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Professional Conduct)

refs.title: Professional Conduct (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: What is an affirmation?

options.text: A solemn declaration with the same legal force as an oath, made without reference to a Supreme Being
options.why: Correct. People with religious or conscientious objections to swearing may affirm instead.

options.text: A weaker statement without legal consequences
options.why: Wrong. A false affirmation is as punishable as a false oath.

options.text: A notary's approval of a document
options.why: Wrong. Notaries don't approve documents.

options.text: A statement made only in court
options.why: Wrong. Affirmations are used in affidavits and many other documents.

explanation: An affirmation is a solemn declaration made by those who object to taking an oath; it has the same legal effect.
source: N.Y. CPLR 2309; DOS Notary Public License Law

refs.title: Definitions: Affirmation (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Definitions: Oath (CPLR 2309(b)) (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: For a jurat, when must the affiant sign?

options.text: In the notary's presence, after (or as part of) taking the oath
options.why: Correct. A jurat certifies the document was subscribed and sworn before the notary.

options.text: Any time before the appointment
options.why: Wrong. That's allowed for acknowledgments, not jurats.

options.text: After leaving the notary's office
options.why: Wrong. The notary must witness the signing.

options.text: Never; the notary signs for them
options.why: Wrong. The affiant must sign personally.

explanation: For an affidavit, the affiant must sign and swear in the notary's presence.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Affidavit, Oath)

refs.title: Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Definitions: Oath (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: Which wording typically appears in a New York jurat?

options.text: "Sworn to before me this ___ day of ____, 20__"
options.why: Correct. That's standard jurat language.

options.text: "On the ___ day of ___ before me personally appeared..."
options.why: Wrong. That opens an acknowledgment certificate.

options.text: "I certify this is a true copy"
options.why: Wrong. New York notaries can't certify copies.

options.text: "Witnessed only, not sworn"
options.why: Wrong. A jurat requires an oath.

explanation: Jurats commonly read "Sworn to before me this ___ day of ____, 20__," followed by the notary's signature and stamp.

refs.title: Definitions: Jurat (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: A person knowingly makes a false statement in an affidavit sworn before a notary. What is the consequence?

options.text: The affiant may be guilty of perjury
options.why: Correct. Swearing falsely is perjury under the Penal Law.

options.text: The notary is automatically guilty of perjury
options.why: Wrong. The notary didn't make the statement (unless they knowingly took part).

options.text: Nothing, because it wasn't in court
options.why: Wrong. Perjury covers false sworn statements outside court too.

options.text: The affidavit becomes an acknowledgment
options.why: Wrong. A false oath doesn't convert the act.

explanation: The person who swears falsely may be guilty of perjury.
source: N.Y. Penal Law art. 210; NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Perjury)

refs.title: Perjury (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 15)
Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: What is a deposition?

options.text: The testimony of a witness taken under oath out of court, reduced to writing
options.why: Correct. Depositions are sworn testimony, usually taken before trial.

options.text: A deed to real property
options.why: Wrong. A deed is a conveyance.

options.text: A notary's application
options.why: Wrong. An application isn't testimony.

options.text: A bank's protest notice
options.why: Wrong. A protest concerns dishonored instruments.

explanation: A deposition is a witness's testimony taken under oath outside court, in writing.

refs.title: Definitions: Deposition (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: May a New York notary administer an oath of office to a public officer?

options.text: Yes; notaries may administer oaths and affirmations generally
options.why: Correct. Executive Law §135 authorizes notaries to administer oaths and affirmations.

options.text: No; only judges may
options.why: Wrong. Notaries are among the officers authorized to give oaths.

options.text: Only for county officers
options.why: Wrong. The power isn't limited to particular offices.

options.text: Only if the officer is a relative
options.why: Wrong. Being related is irrelevant, and could raise impartiality concerns.

explanation: Executive Law §135 authorizes notaries to administer oaths and affirmations.
source: N.Y. Exec. Law §135; N.Y. Pub. Off. Law §10

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §135 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)
Public Officers Law §10 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 13)

question: An affiant arrives with an affidavit already signed and asks the notary to add a jurat. The notary should:

options.text: Administer the oath and have the affiant sign again in the notary's presence
options.why: Correct. The jurat must truthfully say the document was sworn and subscribed before the notary.

options.text: Add the jurat to the existing signature
options.why: Wrong. That falsely certifies a signature the notary didn't witness.

options.text: Convert it to an acknowledgment on their own
options.why: Wrong. Changing the act is not the notary's decision.

options.text: Refuse permanently
options.why: Wrong. Re-signing solves the problem.

explanation: A jurat requires the affiant to swear and subscribe before the notary.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Oath, Affidavit)

refs.title: Definitions: Oath (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)
Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: Who decides between an oath and an affirmation?

options.text: The person taking it
options.why: Correct. It's a matter of the person's own conscience.

options.text: The notary
options.why: Wrong. The notary must respect the person's choice.

options.text: The attorney who drafted the affidavit
options.why: Wrong. The drafter can't impose it.

options.text: The county clerk
options.why: Wrong. The clerk isn't involved.

explanation: The person being sworn chooses whether to swear or affirm.

refs.title: Definitions: Oath (CPLR 2309(b)) (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)
Definitions: Affirmation (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: During an oath, the affiant says, "I'm not sure all of this is true, but I'll sign." The notary should:

options.text: Not complete the jurat, because the affiant hasn't truly sworn the contents are true
options.why: Correct. The oath is meaningless if the affiant openly disclaims its truth.

options.text: Complete it, because truth is the affiant's problem
options.why: Wrong. The notary can't certify an oath that wasn't really given.

options.text: Edit the affidavit to make it accurate
options.why: Wrong. Notaries never edit document contents.

options.text: Complete it as an acknowledgment instead
options.why: Wrong. Switching acts isn't the notary's choice.

explanation: If the affiant won't swear to the truth, there is no valid oath to certify.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Oath)

refs.title: Definitions: Oath (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: Is a notary responsible for checking that an affidavit's statements are true?

options.text: No; the affiant swears to the truth and bears responsibility for it
options.why: Correct. The notary administers the oath and identifies the affiant.

options.text: Yes, always
options.why: Wrong. Notaries have no fact-finding duty.

options.text: Only for immigration affidavits
options.why: Wrong. No document type changes this.

options.text: Only if the notary is an attorney
options.why: Wrong. An attorney-notary's notarial role is the same.

explanation: The notary does not verify the facts in an affidavit.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Affidavit, Oath)

refs.title: Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Definitions: Oath (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: Two affiants sign the same affidavit. What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Identify each affiant, administer the oath to each, and have each sign in the notary's presence
options.why: Correct. Each affiant makes their own sworn statement.

options.text: Swear only the first affiant
options.why: Wrong. The second affiant would be unsworn.

options.text: Have one affiant swear on behalf of both
options.why: Wrong. No one can swear for another person.

options.text: Let the second affiant sign later without the notary
options.why: Wrong. The jurat would be false for the second signature.

explanation: Each affiant must be identified, sworn and sign before the notary.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Oath)

refs.title: Definitions: Oath (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: What does 'subscribed' mean in 'Subscribed and sworn to before me'?

options.text: Signed
options.why: Correct. To subscribe is to sign one's name at the end of a document.

options.text: Paid for
options.why: Wrong. That's a different sense of the word.

options.text: Recorded
options.why: Wrong. Recording is done by a county clerk.

options.text: Read aloud
options.why: Wrong. Reading aloud isn't required.

refs.title: Definitions: Affiant (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
